symptom: Two access switches keep flapping; PCs on VLAN 20 intermittently lose connectivity to the server every few minutes.
topology_note: SW1 and SW2 are connected by two links for redundancy (no EtherChannel configured); both trunk to a core switch.
show_output: show spanning-tree vlan 20 output shows repeated TCN (topology change) events on Fa0/1 and Fa0/2 of SW1; interface counters show high collision/error count on Fa0/2.
expected_fault: Redundant link without EtherChannel is causing a bridging loop / repeated STP topology changes destabilizing the network.
concept_tag: STP topology change / missing EtherChannel

symptom: Half the PCs on VLAN 30 can reach the internet, the other half cannot, despite all having correct IP/mask/gateway.
topology_note: R1 and R2 run HSRP for VLAN 30's gateway 10.30.0.1; R2 was recently rebooted for maintenance.
show_output: show standby brief on R1 shows state Active, priority 110. show standby brief on R2 shows state Standby, priority 100, preempt not configured. R2's WAN link to ISP is actually down.
expected_fault: HSRP did not fail over correctly / R2 lacks a track/preempt config, so traffic routed through R2 (whose WAN link is down) is silently dropped for PCs whose ARP cache points to R2's virtual MAC via unequal load.
concept_tag: HSRP failover misconfiguration (no interface tracking)

symptom: Trunk between two switches passes VLAN 10 traffic fine but VLAN 40 traffic never arrives on the far side.
topology_note: SW1 trunk to SW2 over Gi0/1, both configured as 802.1Q trunks carrying VLANs 10,20,30,40.
show_output: show interfaces trunk on SW1 lists allowed VLANs 1-4094 but show vlan brief on SW2 does not list VLAN 40 at all.
expected_fault: VLAN 40 was never created on SW2 (or was pruned/deleted), so trunked frames for VLAN 40 are dropped at SW2 despite the trunk itself being healthy.
concept_tag: Missing VLAN on remote switch

symptom: A student's laptop connects fine on Monday but is completely blocked from the network on Tuesday after they swapped which port they plugged into.
topology_note: Port security is configured on access ports in the lab with mac address sticky and maximum 1.
show_output: show port-security interface Fa0/5 shows Secure-shutdown (err-disabled) state; violation count 1.
expected_fault: Port security violation: laptop's MAC was learned/sticky on the original port; connecting to a new port under max-1 policy triggered a security violation and error-disabled the new port.
concept_tag: Port security violation / err-disabled port

symptom: Users can browse to internal servers by IP but not by name; external websites work fine by both name and IP.
topology_note: Internal DNS server 10.10.5.5 hosts records for the company's internal domain; external DNS forwarding is configured to 8.8.8.8.
show_output: nslookup for external domains succeeds. nslookup for internal hostnames times out. show run on DNS server config shows forwarder present but no internal zone file loaded.
expected_fault: Internal DNS zone is missing/not loaded on the DNS server, so internal name resolution fails while external forwarding still works.
concept_tag: Missing internal DNS zone

symptom: Branch office can reach HQ server, but responses seem to take an unusually long, inconsistent path and sometimes time out.
topology_note: Branch router has two routes to HQ subnet: one static, one learned via OSPF, both present in the routing table.
show_output: show ip route shows two routes to 172.16.0.0/24 with different next hops and no clear administrative distance difference logged; traceroute shows path oscillating between two different hops on repeated runs.
expected_fault: Routing instability caused by two competing paths with equal/near-equal preference (equal-cost or misconfigured AD) causing route flapping/asymmetric routing.
concept_tag: Route flapping due to competing static/OSPF paths

symptom: Several users behind the same router suddenly cannot reach any external website, though internal resources work fine.
topology_note: Router performs PAT (NAT overload) for ~40 internal hosts using a single public IP with default enabled ports.
show_output: show ip nat translations shows the translation table at a very high entry count; new connection attempts are being dropped. show ip nat statistics shows 'Total translations near limit'.
expected_fault: NAT overload port/translation table exhaustion due to too many simultaneous connections mapped to a single public IP.
concept_tag: NAT/PAT table exhaustion

symptom: Guest Wi-Fi users can browse the internet but corporate Wi-Fi users on the same AP intermittently lose connection and get re-prompted to authenticate.
topology_note: AP broadcasts two SSIDs (Corporate - WPA2-Enterprise/RADIUS, Guest - WPA2-PSK) on the same radio.
show_output: show wireless client shows repeated re-authentication events only for corporate SSID clients; RADIUS server log shows intermittent timeout responses.
expected_fault: RADIUS server response delay/timeout is causing corporate WPA2-Enterprise clients to be periodically de-authenticated, while PSK-based guest clients are unaffected since they don't depend on RADIUS.
concept_tag: RADIUS timeout causing WPA2-Enterprise re-auth failures

symptom: A specific server can be pinged by IT staff but web (HTTP/HTTPS) access to it from the same staff subnet fails.
topology_note: An ACL is applied inbound on the server's VLAN interface intended to restrict access to admin subnet only.
show_output: show access-lists shows a permit icmp entry for the staff subnet followed by an implicit deny; no explicit permit tcp entry exists for port 80/443.
expected_fault: ACL only explicitly permits ICMP; HTTP/HTTPS traffic falls through to the implicit deny at the end of the ACL.
concept_tag: Incomplete ACL missing explicit web traffic permit

symptom: After a switch replacement, several VLANs disappeared network-wide and all switches show only VLAN 1.
topology_note: The new switch was added into the existing VTP domain without checking its VTP configuration revision number first.
show_output: show vtp status on the new switch shows a higher configuration revision number than existing switches, mode Server, domain matches.
expected_fault: The replacement switch had a higher VTP revision number than the rest of the domain, so it overwrote and wiped out the VLAN database network-wide when it joined.
concept_tag: VTP revision number overwrite / VLAN database wipe

symptom: IPv6 hosts on VLAN 50 can ping each other but cannot reach the IPv6 default gateway or anything beyond the local subnet.
topology_note: Router has ipv6 unicast-routing enabled and an IPv6 address configured on the VLAN 50 interface.
show_output: show ipv6 interface brief shows the SVI as 'up/up' but show ipv6 route shows no directly connected route entry, and hosts report no router advertisements received.
expected_fault: Router advertisements are being suppressed (interface configured with ipv6 nd ra suppress) or router IPv6 forwarding is misconfigured, so SLAAC-based hosts never learn a working default gateway.
concept_tag: Suppressed IPv6 router advertisements

symptom: New laptops on VLAN 60 (a newly added floor) never get an IP address and fall back to APIPA (169.254.x.x); VLAN 10 on the same building works fine.
topology_note: DHCP server is centralized on VLAN 10; VLAN 60 is a new VLAN added to the access switch and trunked back to the core/router.
show_output: show ip interface brief on the router shows no ip helper-address configured on the VLAN 60 SVI, while VLAN 10's SVI has one pointing to the DHCP server.
expected_fault: Missing ip helper-address (DHCP relay) on the new VLAN's SVI, so DHCP broadcast requests never reach the centralized DHCP server.
concept_tag: Missing DHCP relay (ip helper-address) on new VLAN

symptom: Site-to-site connectivity between two branches works for small pings but breaks or is very slow for file transfers and large pages.
topology_note: Branches connected via a GRE tunnel over an ISP link with default MTU settings; tunnel interface uses default MTU 1476.
show_output: Small ping (size 100) succeeds through the tunnel; ping with size 1500 and 'do not fragment' set fails/times out. show interface tunnel0 shows MTU 1476.
expected_fault: MTU mismatch/fragmentation issue over the GRE tunnel — large packets exceed the tunnel's effective MTU and are being dropped instead of fragmented (path MTU discovery blocked).
concept_tag: GRE tunnel MTU / fragmentation issue

symptom: A user plugged a small unmanaged switch into two wall jacks in the same room (unaware they're on the same VLAN) and now half the office loses connectivity intermittently.
topology_note: The unmanaged switch creates a physical loop between two access ports on the same access switch; no BPDU guard configured on access ports.
show_output: show spanning-tree vlan 10 shows frequent topology changes; show interfaces on the affected ports shows rapidly increasing broadcast counts.
expected_fault: A user-created physical loop (rogue unmanaged switch bridging two live ports) triggered a broadcast storm; lack of BPDU Guard/loop protection let it happen undetected.
concept_tag: Broadcast storm from unauthorized loop / missing BPDU guard

symptom: Internal clients can resolve internal hostnames correctly but every lookup takes 5-10 seconds before succeeding.
topology_note: Internal DNS server forwards unresolved internal queries to a secondary internal DNS server, then to an external forwarder as a last resort.
show_output: DNS server logs show queries retrying against an unreachable secondary DNS server (10.10.5.6, decommissioned last month) before falling through to the working primary/forwarder path.
expected_fault: Stale forwarder/secondary DNS server entry pointing to a decommissioned host is causing every query to time out against it before falling through to a working resolver.
concept_tag: Stale DNS forwarder causing resolution delay (not failure)

symptom: Staff can ping and browse the web to a partner server, but a specific database application (custom TCP port 1521) never connects.
topology_note: ACL applied on the router interface facing the partner server is meant to allow ping and the database app, but was written in a hurry.
show_output: show access-lists shows: permit icmp any any, permit tcp any any eq 80, permit tcp any any eq 443, deny tcp any any eq 1521, permit ip any any. The specific deny for port 1521 sits above the general permit.
expected_fault: A deny rule for TCP port 1521 was placed above the general permit-any rule, so it matches and blocks the database traffic before the broader permit is ever reached.
concept_tag: ACL rule order - deny placed before general permit

symptom: After two branch offices merged their networks, some internal servers are unreachable from the other branch, while others work fine.
topology_note: Both branches independently used the 192.168.1.0/24 private range before merging; a new WAN link connects them directly without NAT between the two internal networks.
show_output: show ip route on Branch A's router shows a route to 192.168.1.0/24 via the WAN link, but Branch A itself also uses 192.168.1.0/24 internally, creating ambiguous/conflicting routes.
expected_fault: Both branches use the same private IP range (192.168.1.0/24), so traffic meant for the other branch is being misrouted to local devices with the same address (an address overlap requiring NAT between sites).
concept_tag: Overlapping private IP ranges after network merger (double NAT needed)

symptom: Occasionally, a PC on VLAN 10 (Guest) receives traffic meant for VLAN 1, and a network security scan flags unexpected cross-VLAN visibility.
topology_note: Trunk link between SW1 and SW2: SW1's native VLAN is set to 1 (default), SW2's native VLAN was changed to 10 during a Guest network project.
show_output: show interfaks trunk shows Native VLAN: 1 on SW1 and Native VLAN: 10 on SW2 for the same trunk link; CDP native VLAN mismatch warning present in logs.
expected_fault: Native VLAN mismatch between the two ends of the trunk link causes untagged frames to be interpreted as different VLANs on each side, leaking traffic between VLAN 1 and VLAN 10.
concept_tag: Native VLAN mismatch on trunk (security issue)

symptom: Two routers running OSPF show as neighbors but never fully exchange full routing tables; some remote subnets are missing from the routing table.
topology_note: R1 and R2 connect over a point-to-point link running OSPF area 0; R1's interface MTU was recently changed for a QoS project.
show_output: show ip ospf neighbor shows R2 stuck in state EXSTART/EXCHANGE with R1, never reaching FULL. show interfaces shows R1 MTU 1500, R2 MTU 1400.
expected_fault: An MTU mismatch between the two OSPF routers is preventing the neighbor relationship from completing (stuck in EXSTART), so routes are never fully exchanged.
concept_tag: OSPF neighbor stuck due to MTU mismatch

symptom: Two routers running EIGRP on directly connected interfaces can ping each other but never become EIGRP neighbors, and routes aren't shared.
topology_note: R1 and R2 are directly connected; both were configured with EIGRP by two different team members on different days.
show_output: show ip eigrp neighbors is empty on both routers. show run shows R1 configured with 'router eigrp 100' and R2 configured with 'router eigrp 200'.
expected_fault: EIGRP autonomous system (AS) numbers must match between neighbors for them to form a relationship; R1 uses AS 100 and R2 uses AS 200, so they never become neighbors.
concept_tag: EIGRP AS number mismatch preventing neighbor formation

symptom: Most new devices joining VLAN 70 get an IP address fine, but during peak hours (many devices connecting at once) some fail and fall back to APIPA.
topology_note: DHCP server has a scope of 50 addresses configured for VLAN 70, which now has roughly 60 regular daily users plus guest devices.
show_output: show ip dhcp pool statistics shows 'Addresses in use: 50 / Total: 50' during peak hours; DHCP server logs show DHCPNAK / no addresses available errors.
expected_fault: The DHCP scope for VLAN 70 is too small for current demand and is exhausted during peak hours, so new devices can't get an address.
concept_tag: DHCP scope exhaustion

symptom: Employees near the west side of the office report Wi-Fi that connects but is extremely slow and drops frequently, while the east side is fine.
topology_note: Two APs cover the office; a newly installed personal Wi-Fi router (unauthorized) was found broadcasting nearby on an overlapping channel.
show_output: Wireless site survey shows the corporate AP on channel 6 and an unrecognized SSID 'MyHomeWifi' also broadcasting on channel 6 with strong signal in the same area.
expected_fault: A rogue, unauthorized access point broadcasting on the same/overlapping Wi-Fi channel as the corporate AP is causing interference and degraded performance nearby.
concept_tag: Rogue AP / channel interference

symptom: A specific employee cannot connect to the corporate Wi-Fi at all, getting an 'incorrect password' error, while everyone else connects fine.
topology_note: Corporate SSID uses WPA2-PSK (not RADIUS) with a shared password that was rotated last week after a policy change.
show_output: AP association logs show repeated authentication failures from the employee's device MAC address; no other devices show failures.
expected_fault: The employee's device still has the old, pre-rotation Wi-Fi password saved and hasn't been updated with the new shared PSK.
concept_tag: Stale saved Wi-Fi password after PSK rotation

symptom: Voice calls over the office phone system are choppy and cut out specifically when someone is also doing a large file upload, but are fine otherwise.
topology_note: VoIP phones and regular data traffic (including large uploads) share the same uplink with no QoS policy configured.
show_output: show policy-map interface on the uplink shows no QoS policy applied; interface utilization spikes to 100% during large uploads with no traffic prioritization.
expected_fault: Without a QoS policy to prioritize voice traffic, large file uploads consume all available bandwidth on the shared uplink, starving latency-sensitive VoIP traffic and causing choppy calls.
concept_tag: Missing QoS policy causing VoIP degradation under load

symptom: Two devices that should be able to reach a shared printer (but not each other) can now reach each other directly, which violates the intended isolation policy.
topology_note: Private VLAN configured with isolated ports intended to let devices reach only a 'promiscuous' printer port, not each other.
show_output: show interfaces private-vlan mapping shows the two device ports incorrectly configured as 'community' ports (which can talk to each other) instead of 'isolated' ports.
expected_fault: The ports were configured as community (which allows same-group devices to talk to each other) instead of isolated (which blocks it), breaking the intended isolation policy.
concept_tag: Private VLAN port type misconfiguration (community vs isolated)

symptom: A newly added switch, meant to extend VLAN 20 to a new room, shows the new room's PCs able to reach each other but nothing beyond that switch.
topology_note: The uplink port connecting the new switch back to the main switch was configured as a regular access port instead of a trunk.
show_output: show interfaces switchport on the uplink port shows Administrative Mode: static access, Access Vlan: 20, Trunking Encapsulation: N/A.
expected_fault: The uplink port between the new switch and the main switch was left as an access port instead of being configured as a trunk, so only a single VLAN's untagged traffic can pass, cutting off the new switch from other VLANs/the rest of the network as intended.
concept_tag: Switch uplink left as access port instead of trunk

symptom: Employees working from inside the office are sent to an outdated version of the internal wiki page, while remote employees on VPN see the current version.
topology_note: Split-horizon DNS is configured so internal requests for wiki.company.com should resolve to an internal server IP, and external/VPN requests resolve to a cloud-hosted IP.
show_output: nslookup for wiki.company.com from inside the office returns 10.10.9.9 (old internal server, no longer updated). nslookup from a VPN client returns the correct cloud IP.
expected_fault: The internal DNS view (split-horizon) still points wiki.company.com to the old, no-longer-maintained internal server IP, while the external view was correctly updated to the new cloud-hosted address.
concept_tag: Split-horizon DNS view not updated internally

symptom: Two internal servers on different VLANs that should communicate directly are instead having their traffic unexpectedly translated, breaking an application that depends on seeing the real source IP.
topology_note: NAT is configured on the router with an ACL intended to match only internet-bound traffic, but the ACL was written too broadly.
show_output: show ip nat translations shows translation entries for source and destination IPs that are both internal/private addresses. show access-lists for the NAT ACL shows 'permit ip any any' instead of a scoped internal-to-internet match.
expected_fault: The NAT ACL is too broad (matches any traffic instead of just internet-bound traffic), causing internal-to-internal traffic between the two servers to be unintentionally translated as well.
concept_tag: Overly broad NAT ACL translating internal-to-internal traffic

symptom: A PC that was working fine suddenly loses network connectivity, and shortly after, another PC on the same VLAN also starts having intermittent connectivity issues.
topology_note: A new PC was manually assigned a static IP address by IT without checking the DHCP scope or existing assignments.
show_output: Windows shows an 'IP address conflict' warning on both PCs' event logs; both devices show the same IP address 10.10.2.50 in ARP tables at different times.
expected_fault: A statically assigned IP address on the new PC conflicts with an address already in use (assigned by DHCP or another static assignment), causing intermittent connectivity for both devices as they fight over the same address.
concept_tag: Duplicate/conflicting IP address assignment

symptom: A newly configured PC can ping its own gateway and a couple of nearby devices, but not most of the rest of its own VLAN.
topology_note: PC was manually configured with IP 10.10.4.50 but with an incorrect subnet mask of 255.255.255.240 instead of the intended 255.255.255.0.
show_output: ipconfig on the PC shows IP 10.10.4.50, mask 255.255.255.240. Devices it can reach fall within 10.10.4.48-10.10.4.63; devices outside that narrow range are unreachable directly.
expected_fault: An incorrect (too narrow) subnet mask on the PC makes it think most of its own VLAN is on a different network, so it tries to route to those devices via the gateway instead of talking to them directly, and fails.
concept_tag: Incorrect subnet mask limiting effective local network size

symptom: PCs on VLAN 80 cannot reach a file server on VLAN 10 at all, not even a ping succeeds, despite VLAN 80 appearing correctly configured on the access switch.
topology_note: Two issues exist simultaneously: VLAN 80 was never added to the trunk's allowed VLAN list between the access switch and the core switch, AND the router's ACL for VLAN 80 only permits traffic to VLAN 20, not VLAN 10.
show_output: show interfaces trunk on the access switch shows allowed VLANs list does not include 80. Separately, show access-lists on the router shows an ACL applied to VLAN 80's interface permitting traffic only to 10.10.20.0/24 (VLAN 20), with implicit deny for everything else including VLAN 10.
expected_fault: Two independent faults are both blocking connectivity: VLAN 80 is pruned from the trunk's allowed VLAN list (Layer 2 issue), and even if that's fixed, the router ACL for VLAN 80 doesn't permit traffic to VLAN 10 (Layer 3/4 issue) - both must be fixed for connectivity to work.
concept_tag: Combined Layer 2 (VLAN pruned from trunk) and Layer 3/4 (restrictive ACL) fault

symptom: Devices on the newly added VLAN 90 cannot get a DHCP address, and even a PC manually assigned a static IP on VLAN 90 cannot reach a server on VLAN 10.
topology_note: Two issues exist: the VLAN 90 SVI on the router is missing an ip helper-address for DHCP relay, AND the router is also missing a route back to VLAN 10 from a recent static routing change that wasn't fully applied.
show_output: show run interface vlan90 shows no ip helper-address configured. Separately, show ip route shows no entry for the VLAN 10 subnet at all on the router handling VLAN 90's traffic.
expected_fault: Two independent faults exist: missing DHCP relay (ip helper-address) prevents automatic addressing, and a missing static/dynamic route to VLAN 10's subnet prevents connectivity even with a manually assigned IP - both must be fixed.
concept_tag: Combined missing DHCP relay and missing route fault

symptom: All users behind a branch router suddenly lose internet access; even after some users disconnect to reduce load, a few users still cannot get through.
topology_note: Two issues occurred close together: the NAT overload translation table filled up during a traffic spike, AND a recently added ACL meant to block a specific malicious IP range was written too broadly and is blocking a chunk of legitimate return traffic too.
show_output: show ip nat statistics shows 'translations near limit' during the spike. Separately, show access-lists shows a deny rule matching a wide IP range (10.0.0.0/8 instead of the intended single malicious /32 address) applied inbound on the WAN interface.
expected_fault: Two independent faults compound the outage: NAT/PAT table exhaustion during a traffic spike caused temporary failures for many users, and a separately, overly broad ACL (written to block one malicious IP but matching a huge range) is blocking legitimate return traffic for a subset of users even after the NAT load drops.
concept_tag: Combined NAT exhaustion and overly broad security ACL fault

symptom: A user's connection to a server is technically 'up' but painfully slow and shows a high number of errors, unlike everyone else on the same switch.
topology_note: The user's PC network card is configured for 100 Mbps full-duplex, but the switch port it connects to auto-negotiated down to 100 Mbps half-duplex due to a firmware quirk.
show_output: show interfaces Fa0/12 shows: 100Mb/s, half-duplex, and a rapidly increasing counter for 'late collisions' and 'runts', unlike other ports on the same switch showing full-duplex with no errors.
expected_fault: A duplex mismatch between the PC (full-duplex) and the switch port (half-duplex) is causing collisions and errors, resulting in a connection that appears 'up' but performs very poorly.
concept_tag: Duplex mismatch causing degraded performance

symptom: A new employee's laptop can reach every other device on its own VLAN but cannot reach anything outside the subnet, including the internet.
topology_note: Laptop was manually assigned a static IP by IT; correct IP and subnet mask, but the default gateway field was typed incorrectly during setup.
show_output: ipconfig on the laptop shows IP 10.10.6.50, mask 255.255.255.0, default gateway 10.10.6.99 - but the actual router interface for this VLAN is 10.10.6.1. show arp on the router has no entry for 10.10.6.99, confirming an incorrect default-gateway configuration on the host.
expected_fault: The laptop was configured with an incorrect default gateway address (10.10.6.99) that doesn't correspond to any real device on the subnet, instead of the router's actual interface address (10.10.6.1), so all off-subnet traffic has nowhere to go.
concept_tag: Incorrect default gateway configuration on host
